milestone: Milestone 1: Technical Understanding and Research Framing

entries.objective: Prepare a structured technical understanding for the first milestone of the seminar topic.
entries.prompt: I am preparing the first milestone for my seminar topic, List-Based Scheduling for High-Level Synthesis. I want to organize my understanding in a clear technical way with problem statement, motivation, core idea, algorithm, assumptions, resource aspects, and open questions. Please help me make it suitable for a milestone submission, not like a polished final paper.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI helped structure the milestone into concise technical sections: problem statement, motivation, core idea, formal model, pseudocode, small scheduling example, assumptions, runtime and memory aspects, embedded-system relevance, and feedback questions.

actions: Checked that the milestone follows the required Milestone 1 structure: technical problem, main idea, algorithm/formalism, assumptions, resource aspects, and unclear points.
Checked that the text is written as structured technical notes rather than polished final-paper prose.
Checked that the student name and ID are included correctly in the milestone and protocol files.

issues: The first version had the student ID missing in some files, so the corrected version explicitly includes Student ID 2220070.
The AI prompt was rewritten in a natural student-style form instead of a command-style form.
The technical details should still be checked against the assigned textbook chapter or lecture slides before final submission.

entries.reflection: This interaction helped transform the topic into a clear technical briefing. I used the structure and explanations, but the final version should still be reviewed with the course material and my own implementation results.

entries.objective: Clarify the formal model used in list-based scheduling for HLS.
entries.prompt: For the same milestone, I also need to explain the basic formal model behind list-based scheduling. I want the explanation to be understandable for a beginner, but still technical enough for a seminar milestone. Please include the data-flow graph, precedence constraints, resource constraints, mobility, and latency.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI explained the data-flow graph G=(V,E), precedence constraints, resource constraints, schedule latency, ASAP/ALAP timing, and mobility in a compact technical form.

actions: Checked that the precedence constraint prevents dependent operations from starting too early.
Checked that the resource constraint limits the number of simultaneously active operations of the same resource type.
Checked that mobility is described as ALAP minus ASAP.

issues: The model is simplified and does not deeply cover memory-port conflicts, branches, or loops.
The final seminar paper may need more references and a deeper discussion of real HLS tools.

integration.section: Formal Model; ASAP, ALAP, and Mobility

entries.reflection: The formal model made the scheduling topic easier to connect with the implementation example and later waveform explanation.

entries.objective: Create a small example that connects the theory to implementation.
entries.prompt: I want to include a small example for the milestone using the expression z = (a+b) * (c+d) + e. Please help me show how the schedule changes when I use one ALU compared with two ALUs, so that the resource-latency tradeoff becomes clear.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI prepared a small scheduling example showing that one ALU plus one multiplier gives a 4-cycle schedule, while two ALUs plus one multiplier can give a 3-cycle schedule.

actions: Checked that v3 depends on both v1 and v2.
Checked that v4 depends on v3.
Checked that the two additions can run in parallel only when two ALUs are available.

issues: The example assumes one-cycle operations and ignores memory access.
The example is useful for explanation but is not enough to represent all real HLS scheduling problems.

entries.reflection: The example gives a simple way to explain why resource constraints matter in list-based scheduling.
